title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.1 Models of the Earth system
In this lecture we deal with prognostic modelling of the physics of the Earth and the atmosphere. Before we write down any equation, we clarify what models are for.

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
TipThink first: what are models good for?






Prediction. A model simulates the past and present state of a system and predicts its future state. Weather and climate models predict the future state of the atmosphere and the ocean. This is what we call prognostic modelling.
Filling gaps. Measurements of temperature, rain or water levels are never continuous in space and time, not even from satellites. Models interpolate between locations and between measurement times. Nobody can measure the future, so looking ahead always needs a model that extrapolates.
Seeing the unobservable. Models give access to variables for which no sensor exists, or which cannot be measured with the required accuracy or coverage, for example the water stored in the deep subsurface.
Virtual experiments. Models allow experiments that are impossible, too expensive or too dangerous in reality: doubling atmospheric CO2, removing a mountain range, moving an earthquake source.
Understanding. Models help to understand complex systems and their feedbacks, because every process can be switched on and off.










TipThink first: what types of models exist, and what are their strengths?













Type
Strength
Weakness




Analog (laboratory experiment)
It is real
Needs a laboratory and often much money; valid only in the range of the experiment; scaling to the real system is difficult


Statistical, including machine learning
Works without knowing the governing laws; fast once trained
Needs much data; based on assumptions that are hard to check; unreliable outside the range of the training data


Mathematical (physics-based)
Based on conservation laws, therefore able to extrapolate
Based on simplifying assumptions; parameters are often unknown at the scale of the model; needs applied mathematics and computing



This lecture treats mathematical models. The three types are increasingly combined, for example when a machine-learning model is trained on the output of a physics-based model (Chapter 22).




1.1.1 A first mathematical model
A very familiar physical model is Newton’s second law, \(m a = F\). Written as a differential equation it reads
\[
m \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 u}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = F\!\left(t, u, \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t}\right),
\tag{1.1}\]
where \(u(t)\) is the position of a particle at time \(t\) and \(F\) is the force acting on it. Many problems in science and engineering have this form: an equation that contains one or more derivatives of an unknown function. To model the motion of the particle we have to find the function \(u(t)\) that satisfies Equation 1.1.
Throughout the lecture \(u\) denotes the unknown. Depending on the problem it is a position, a temperature, a pressure, a water depth or a vector of all of these.


1.1.2 Prognostic and diagnostic equations
A prognostic equation contains a time derivative of the unknown. It states how fast the state changes, and therefore allows us to step from the state now to the state a moment later:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \mathcal{F}(u, t).
\tag{1.2}\]
A diagnostic equation contains no time derivative. It relates variables at the same instant. The ideal gas law \(p = \rho R T\) and hydrostatic balance \(\partial p / \partial z = -\rho g\) are diagnostic equations of atmospheric models.
A prognostic model consists of prognostic equations for the variables that carry the memory of the system, the state, together with diagnostic equations for everything that follows from the state. The mathematical task is an initial value problem: given the state at \(t = 0\), find the state at later times.








Model
Prognostic variables (examples)
Equations




Numerical weather prediction, climate
wind, temperature, pressure or density, humidity
conservation of momentum, energy and mass in a rotating, stratified fluid


Ocean circulation
currents, temperature, salinity, sea surface height
the same, for sea water


Groundwater and soil hydrology
pressure head or water content
conservation of mass with Darcy’s law


Seismic wave propagation
particle velocity, stress
conservation of momentum with a stress–strain relation



All these equations are derived in the same way, from the conservation of mass, momentum and energy (Chapter 2), and they are solved with the same small set of numerical methods. That is why meteorologists and geophysicists can share this lecture.

section: 1.2 From physical law to computer code
text:
1.2 From physical law to computer code
Almost no prognostic model of a real system can be solved with pencil and paper. We have to solve it numerically, which means that a simulation result is separated from reality by a chain of steps:

Physical system. The atmosphere, an aquifer, the crust.
Conceptual model. Which processes matter, which are neglected, where the boundaries of the domain are.
Mathematical model. Differential equations with initial and boundary conditions and parameters.
Discretization. The continuous equations are replaced by algebraic equations for a finite number of unknowns.
Solution algorithm. The algebraic equations are solved, often only approximately.
Implementation. The algorithm is written as a program.
Simulation and evaluation. The program is run and its result is compared with observations.

Every step introduces errors. The lecture is mainly about steps 4 to 6, but you will only be able to judge a result if you keep the whole chain in mind.

1.2.1 The central idea: replace derivatives by differences
A computer can add, subtract, multiply and divide. It cannot differentiate. The simplest way to translate a differential equation into arithmetic is the finite difference method, which replaces a derivative by a difference quotient, for example
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t} \approx \frac{u(t + \Delta t) - u(t)}{\Delta t},
\tag{1.3}\]
where \(\Delta t\) is the time step. The derivative is the limit of the right hand side for \(\Delta t \to 0\). On a computer \(\Delta t\) stays finite, and this is the origin of the discretization error.
As an example take the decay equation
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t} = -k u, \qquad u(0) = u_0,
\tag{1.4}\]
which describes radioactive decay, the cooling of a body or the emptying of a linear reservoir. Its exact solution is \(u(t) = u_0 e^{-kt}\). We insert Equation 1.3, write \(u_n\) for the approximation of \(u(n \Delta t)\) and solve for the new value:
\[
u_{n+1} = u_n - k \, \Delta t \, u_n .
\tag{1.5}\]
This is a complete prognostic model. Starting from \(u_0\) it produces the state at all later times using only multiplication and subtraction.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

k, u0, t_end = 1.0, 1.0, 4.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
t_exact = np.linspace(0, t_end, 200)
ax.plot(t_exact, u0 * np.exp(-k * t_exact), "k", label="exact")

for dt in [1.0, 0.5, 0.1]:
    n_steps = int(round(t_end / dt))
    u = np.empty(n_steps + 1)
    u[0] = u0
    for n in range(n_steps):
        u[n + 1] = u[n] - k * dt * u[n]
    ax.plot(dt * np.arange(n_steps + 1), u, "o-", ms=3, label=rf"$\Delta t$ = {dt}")
    error = abs(u[-1] - u0 * np.exp(-k * t_end))
    print(f"dt = {dt:4.1f}: error at t = {t_end:.0f} is {error:.4f}")

ax.set_xlabel("$t$")
ax.set_ylabel("$u$")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

dt =  1.0: error at t = 4 is 0.0183
dt =  0.5: error at t = 4 is 0.0144
dt =  0.1: error at t = 4 is 0.0035








Figure 1.1: Numerical solution of the decay equation with the forward difference for three time steps, compared with the exact solution.





Figure 1.1 shows the behaviour we hope for: the smaller the time step, the closer the numerical solution is to the exact one. It also raises the questions that occupy us for the rest of the semester.






TipTry it



The code below runs in your browser. Change the time step dt and press Run Code. Try 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0. At which value does the numerical solution stop decaying?









How fast does the error decrease when \(\Delta t\) decreases? (Accuracy)
With \(\Delta t = 1\) the numerical solution drops to zero in one step. What happens for \(\Delta t = 3\)? (Stability)
Is there a better formula than Equation 1.5 for the same cost? (Efficiency)



1.2.2 A first analysis
For this simple model the first two questions can be answered on paper. Equation 1.5 multiplies the solution by the same factor in every step, \(u_{n+1} = (1 - k \Delta t) \, u_n\). Applying it \(n\) times,
\[
u_1 = (1 - k \Delta t) \, u_0, \quad
u_2 = (1 - k \Delta t)^2 \, u_0, \quad \dots, \quad
u_n = (1 - k \Delta t)^n \, u_0 .
\tag{1.6}\]
The exact solution is multiplied in every step by \(e^{-k \Delta t}\), since \(u(t + \Delta t) = u_0 e^{-k (t + \Delta t)} = e^{-k \Delta t} \, u(t)\). The Taylor series of this factor is
\[
e^{-k \Delta t} = 1 - k \Delta t + \frac{(k \Delta t)^2}{2} - \dots
\]
The numerical factor \(1 - k \Delta t\) consists of its first two terms.
Accuracy. In one step the numerical and the exact factor differ by \((k \Delta t)^2 / 2\). To reach a fixed time \(t\) we need \(n = t / \Delta t\) steps, so the errors add up to something proportional to \(n \, (k \Delta t)^2 \propto \Delta t\). The error at a fixed time is proportional to the time step: halving \(\Delta t\) halves the error.
Stability. The behaviour of \(u_n = (1 - k \Delta t)^n u_0\) depends only on the size of the factor.








Time step
Factor \(1 - k \Delta t\)
Numerical solution




\(k \Delta t < 1\)
between 0 and 1
decays monotonically, as the exact solution


\(k \Delta t = 1\)
0
zero after one step


\(1 < k \Delta t < 2\)
between \(-1\) and 0
decays, but changes sign in every step


\(k \Delta t > 2\)
below \(-1\)
oscillates and grows without bound



For \(k \Delta t > 2\) the numerical solution has nothing in common with the exact one. The scheme is unstable. The time step of this scheme is therefore limited by the fastest process in the model, not by the accuracy we want. This observation, generalised to systems and to partial differential equations, is one of the main themes of the lecture (Chapter 6).

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.3 Sources of error and uncertainty






TipThink first: which errors occur when a numerical model is developed and applied?





Collect your own list before reading on, and sort it by the step of the modelling chain at which the error arises.



The following table sorts the errors by their origin (after Wick 2020).








Origin
Error
Description




Conceptual and mathematical model
Model error
Processes are missing or simplified, for example a linear equation replaces a nonlinear one. Found only by comparison with observations and by careful reasoning.



Homogenization error
A model at full resolution is replaced by an averaged one; processes smaller than the grid are represented by parameters (parametrization, Chapter 18).



Regularization error
An ill-posed problem is modified so that it becomes well-posed.


Data
Data error
Initial conditions, boundary conditions and parameters come from measurements and are uncertain and incomplete.



Reference error
The observations used for evaluation are themselves inaccurate.


Discretization
Discretization error
Continuous functions are represented by a finite number of values.



Interpolation error
Values between grid points are obtained from simpler functions.


Solution algorithm
Iteration error
Iterative algorithms are stopped after a finite number of steps.


Computer
Round-off error
A computer represents only a finite set of numbers.


Implementation
Bugs
Some make the program abort, which is the harmless case. Others produce results that look plausible and are wrong.



Two remarks help to keep this list in proportion.
First, the errors are of very different size, and the total error is dominated by the largest contribution. If the parameters of a groundwater model are known only within a factor of ten, it is pointless to reduce the discretization error to 0.01 %. Deciding which error dominates is a central task of numerical modelling.
Second, errors in the data are of two kinds. Epistemic uncertainty comes from lack of knowledge and can in principle be reduced by more measurements. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from variability that is random for all practical purposes. Both are treated by running the model many times (Chapter 8).
Of all these errors, the discretization, iteration and round-off errors and the bugs are the ones that numerical methods control. The rest of this unit treats round-off; the discretization error is the subject of most of the following units.

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.4 Floating point arithmetic and round-off

1.4.1 How a computer stores real numbers
A computer stores a real number as a floating point number
\[
x = \pm \, m \cdot 2^{e},
\]
with a significand \(m\) and an exponent \(e\) that each occupy a fixed number of bits. Python and NumPy use by default the double precision format of the IEEE 754 standard with 64 bits, of which 53 hold the significand. This has three consequences (Goldberg 1991).

Finite precision. A double carries about 16 significant decimal digits. The distance between 1 and the next larger floating point number is the machine epsilon, \(\varepsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\).
Finite range. The largest double is about \(1.8 \times 10^{308}\). Larger results overflow to inf.
Most decimal fractions are not representable. In base 2 the number 0.1 has infinitely many digits, as 1/3 has in base 10, and is rounded when it is stored.


import numpy as np

print("machine epsilon:        ", np.finfo(float).eps)
print("1 + eps/2 == 1:         ", 1.0 + np.finfo(float).eps / 2 == 1.0)
print("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3:       ", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print("0.1 + 0.2 =             ", repr(0.1 + 0.2))
print("largest double:         ", np.finfo(float).max)
print("single precision epsilon:", np.finfo(np.float32).eps)

machine epsilon:         2.220446049250313e-16
1 + eps/2 == 1:          True
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3:        False
0.1 + 0.2 =              0.30000000000000004
largest double:          1.7976931348623157e+308
single precision epsilon: 1.1920929e-07


Every arithmetic operation therefore returns the exact result rounded to the nearest floating point number, with a relative error of at most \(\varepsilon / 2\). Two rules follow immediately.

Never test floating point numbers for equality. Test whether their difference is small, for example with np.isclose.
Single precision has only about 7 significant digits. Weather and climate models nevertheless increasingly use it, because it halves memory and data transfer. Whether this is safe has to be shown for each algorithm.



1.4.2 Loss of significance
A relative error of \(10^{-16}\) sounds harmless, and for a single operation it is. It becomes dangerous when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted. The leading digits cancel, and the result consists mostly of the rounding errors of the operands. Consider
\[
f(x) = \frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} \;\to\; \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{for } x \to 0 .
\]

def f_naive(x):
    return (1 - np.cos(x)) / x**2

def f_stable(x):
    return 2 * np.sin(x / 2) ** 2 / x**2

for x in [1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8]:
    print(f"x = {x:.0e}:  naive {f_naive(x):.10f}   stable {f_stable(x):.10f}")

x = 1e-02:  naive 0.4999958333   stable 0.4999958333
x = 1e-04:  naive 0.4999999970   stable 0.4999999996
x = 1e-06:  naive 0.5000444503   stable 0.5000000000
x = 1e-08:  naive 0.0000000000   stable 0.5000000000


For \(x = 10^{-8}\) the first formula returns 0 instead of 0.5: \(\cos x\) differs from 1 by \(5 \times 10^{-17}\), which is less than the machine epsilon, so it is stored as exactly 1. The second formula uses the identity \(1 - \cos x = 2 \sin^2(x/2)\), is mathematically identical and avoids the subtraction.
This has a direct consequence for our central idea. The difference quotient Equation 1.3 subtracts two numbers that become more and more equal as the step decreases. Making the step ever smaller therefore does not make a finite difference ever more accurate. We quantify this in Chapter 3.


1.4.3 Conditioning
Loss of significance is an example of a more general notion. A problem is well-conditioned if small relative changes of the input cause small relative changes of the result, and ill-conditioned if they cause large ones. The amplification factor is the condition number \(\kappa\).
For the evaluation of a function \(f(x)\) it follows from the Taylor series. A small change \(\delta x\) of the input changes the result by \(\delta f \approx f'(x) \, \delta x\). We divide by \(f\) and expand with \(x\) to obtain relative changes on both sides:
\[
\frac{\delta f}{f} \approx \frac{f'(x) \, \delta x}{f(x)}
= \underbrace{\frac{x \, f'(x)}{f(x)}}_{\pm \kappa} \; \frac{\delta x}{x} ,
\qquad
\kappa = \left| \frac{x \, f'(x)}{f(x)} \right| .
\]
The problem. We apply this to the example above, \(f(x) = (1 - \cos x)/x^2\). For small \(x\) the Taylor series of the cosine gives
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{x^2}{24} + \dots, \qquad
f'(x) \approx -\frac{x}{12},
\]
and therefore
\[
\kappa_f = \left| \frac{x \, f'(x)}{f(x)} \right| \approx \frac{x^2 / 12}{1/2} = \frac{x^2}{6} .
\]
For \(x = 10^{-8}\) this is about \(10^{-17}\). The problem is extremely well-conditioned: a small relative error in \(x\) has almost no effect on \(f\). The failure of f_naive therefore cannot be blamed on the problem.
The algorithm. f_naive computes \(f\) in steps, and each step is a problem of its own with its own condition number. First it computes \(c = \cos x\). The result is rounded, so \(c\) carries a relative error of up to \(\varepsilon\). Then it computes \(h(c) = 1 - c\). With the same formula, now for the input \(c\),
\[
\kappa_h = \left| \frac{c \, h'(c)}{h(c)} \right| = \frac{|c|}{|1 - c|} .
\]
For small \(x\) the Taylor series \(\cos x = 1 - x^2/2 + x^4/24 - \dots\) gives \(c \approx 1\) and \(1 - c = x^2/2 - x^4/24 + \dots \approx x^2/2\), hence
\[
\kappa_h \approx \frac{1}{x^2 / 2} = \frac{2}{x^2} .
\]
For \(x = 10^{-8}\) this is \(2 \times 10^{16}\). The rounding error \(\varepsilon \approx 10^{-16}\) of \(c\) is amplified to a relative error of order one: no correct digit remains. f_stable computes \(\sin(x/2)\), squares it and divides by \(x^2\). These steps have condition numbers of about 1 and 2, so the rounding errors stay at the level of \(\varepsilon\).

eps = np.finfo(float).eps
print("     x   kappa problem   kappa step 1-cos x   predicted error   actual error")
for x in [1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8]:
    kappa_f = x**2 / 6                                     # the problem f
    c = np.cos(x)
    kappa_h = abs(c) / abs(1 - c) if c != 1 else np.inf    # the step 1 - c in f_naive
    predicted = kappa_h * eps                              # bound for the relative error of f_naive
    actual = abs(f_naive(x) - f_stable(x)) / f_stable(x)   # f_stable serves as the exact value
    print(f"{x:6.0e}   {kappa_f:13.1e}   {kappa_h:18.1e}   {predicted:15.1e}   {actual:12.1e}")

     x   kappa problem   kappa step 1-cos x   predicted error   actual error
 1e-02         1.7e-05              2.0e+04           4.4e-12        2.9e-13
 1e-04         1.7e-09              2.0e+08           4.4e-08        5.2e-09
 1e-06         1.7e-13              2.0e+12           4.4e-04        8.9e-05
 1e-08         1.7e-17                  inf               inf        1.0e+00


The last two columns compare the error predicted by the condition number of the step \(1 - c\), \(\kappa_h \, \varepsilon\), with the actual relative error of f_naive, for which the result of f_stable serves as the exact value. The prediction is an upper bound, since the rounding error of \(\cos x\) is usually smaller than \(\varepsilon\); it lies within a factor of about 10 of the actual error. Above all, it explains why the error grows by a factor of \(10^4\) each time \(x\) shrinks by a factor of 100. For \(x = 10^{-8}\) the stored value of \(\cos x\) is exactly 1: the step \(1 - c\) has lost all information, which the infinite condition number expresses, and the relative error is 100 %.
Conditioning and stability. Conditioning is a property of the problem. It must be distinguished from the stability of an algorithm. An algorithm is unstable if it amplifies errors more than the problem itself does, typically because it contains an ill-conditioned intermediate step that the problem does not need. Here the problem is well-conditioned, f_naive is unstable because of the step \(1 - \cos x\), and f_stable is stable. For an ill-conditioned problem, in contrast, no algorithm helps; the problem itself has to be reformulated.
We meet the condition number again for linear systems of equations, where the same definition leads to the condition number of a matrix (Chapter 4, Chapter 11), and ill-conditioning in its most famous geophysical form, the limited predictability of weather (Chapter 8).

section: 1.5 Concepts that return in every unit
text:
1.5 Concepts that return in every unit
A few concepts apply to all numerical methods of this lecture. We introduce them informally here and make them precise in Chapter 6.

Approximation

The exact solution \(u\) is not available. We compute an approximation \(\tilde u\) and need to know how far it is from \(u\).

Consistency

A method is consistent if the discrete equations approach the differential equation when the grid spacing and the time step go to zero.

Stability

A method is stable if errors, for example round-off errors, do not grow without bound during the computation. Unstable methods typically show oscillations that grow in time. It is therefore important to know from the physics whether oscillations are to be expected.

Convergence

A method converges if the numerical solution approaches the exact solution when the grid spacing and the time step go to zero. The rate at which it does so is the order of the method.

Efficiency

The accuracy reached for a given amount of computing time, memory and energy. A method of higher order is often, but not always, more efficient.

Well-posedness

A property of the mathematical problem: a solution exists, it is unique, and it depends continuously on the data (Chapter 2). A numerical method cannot repair a problem that is not well-posed.

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.6 Verification and validation
Two questions must be asked of every model (Oberkampf and Roy 2010).
Verification: are we solving the equations right? This is a mathematical question. It is answered by comparing the numerical solution with exact solutions and by checking that the error decreases at the expected rate when the grid is refined. Verification concerns discretization, algorithm and code, and it can be completed.
Validation: are we solving the right equations? This is a physical question. It is answered by comparing the simulation with observations. Validation concerns the conceptual and mathematical model and the data, and it is never complete, because a model can only be shown to agree with the observations available so far.
The order matters. A model that has not been verified cannot be validated, because agreement with observations may result from errors that compensate each other. In this lecture you verify every program you write.

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.7 Working practice
Numerical modelling is to a large part work on paper. Classifying the problem, deriving the discrete equations, and writing down the grid, the indices and the boundary conditions come first. Programming, debugging and plotting are the smaller part, and they go quickly when the paper work is complete.
The following habits save most of the time that is usually lost.

Simplify. Start with the lowest resolution, the simplest boundary and initial conditions and constant coefficients. Add one complication at a time.
Know the answer in advance. Test first on a problem with a known solution. For a linear system with five unknowns you can check every number by hand.
Write functions and test them. A function that does one thing can be tested once and then trusted: on a problem with a known answer, and again after every change. In the exercises you collect your functions in your own module toolbox.py and reuse them in later sheets and in the project.
Use version control. With git every working state of a program can be recovered, and every result can be attributed to the version of the code that produced it.
Make results reproducible. A figure should be produced by a script from the raw output, without manual steps. All figures in this script are produced by the code shown next to them.

title: 1  What is prognostic modelling?
text:
1.8 Summary

A prognostic model predicts the future state of a system from its present state with equations that contain time derivatives. Diagnostic equations relate variables at the same time.
A simulation result is separated from reality by a chain of steps: conceptual model, mathematical model, discretization, algorithm, implementation. Each contributes errors, and the largest contribution dominates.
The basic idea of discretization is to replace derivatives by difference quotients. The resulting discretization error decreases with the step.
Floating point numbers have about 16 significant digits. Subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys most of them.
Verification checks the solution of the equations, validation checks the equations. Verification comes first.

title: 2  Governing equations and their classification
text:
2.1 Vector calculus recap
Numerical modelling starts on paper with the classification of the problem. The type of an equation decides which numerical methods work and which fail. This unit provides the language: the operators of vector calculus, the conservation laws built from them, the classification of the resulting equations, and the equations of this lecture with their types.
crumbs: 2  Governing equations and their classification

title: 2  Governing equations and their classification
text:
2.1.1 Derivatives
If the unknown depends on a single variable, for example \(u(t)\), its rate of change is the ordinary derivative \(\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}t\). If it depends on several variables, for example \(u(x, t)\), the partial derivatives \(\partial u/\partial t\) and \(\partial u/\partial x\) give the rate of change with respect to one variable while the others are held fixed. Derivatives of order \(n\) are written \(\mathrm{d}^n u/\mathrm{d}t^n\) and \(\partial^n u/\partial x^n\). We also use the short forms \(u_t\), \(u_x\), \(u_{xx}\).


2.1.2 Vectors
A vector in the plane is written \(\vec v = v_1 \vec i + v_2 \vec j\), in space \(\vec v = v_1 \vec i + v_2 \vec j + v_3 \vec k\), where \(\vec i, \vec j, \vec k\) are the unit vectors along the coordinate axes. Its magnitude is
\[
\| \vec v \| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2},
\]
and the unit vector in the direction of \(\vec v\) is \(\vec v / \|\vec v\|\).


2.1.3 The gradient
The gradient of a scalar field \(f(x, y, z)\) is the vector
\[
\operatorname{grad} f = \nabla f =
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \vec i +
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \vec j +
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \vec k .
\]
It has two geometric properties, shown in Figure 2.1.

\(\nabla f\) points in the direction in which \(f\) increases fastest, and is perpendicular to the contour of \(f\) through the point.
\(\|\nabla f\|\) is the rate of change in that direction. It is large where the contours are close together.

In physics, gradients drive fluxes: heat flows down the temperature gradient, groundwater flows down the gradient of hydraulic head, and the pressure gradient accelerates the wind.








Figure 2.1: Contours of \(f(x, y) = x + e^{y}\) and its gradient vectors. The vectors are perpendicular to the contours and longer where the contours are closer.











TipExercise: gradient of \(f(x, y) = x + e^{y}\) at the point \((1, 1)\)





\(\nabla f = \vec i + e^{y} \vec j\), so \(\nabla f(1, 1) = \vec i + e \, \vec j\). The maximum rate of change at this point is \(\|\nabla f\| = \sqrt{1 + e^2} \approx 2.90\).





2.1.4 The divergence
The divergence of a vector field \(\vec F\) measures the outflow per unit volume at a point. Geometrically, it is the flux out of a small closed surface \(S\) around the point, divided by the enclosed volume \(V\), in the limit of vanishing volume:
\[
\operatorname{div} \vec F = \nabla \cdot \vec F =
\lim_{V \to 0} \frac{1}{V} \oint_S \vec F \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec A .
\tag{2.1}\]
Here \(\mathrm{d}\vec A\) is the surface element with the direction of the outward normal. In Cartesian coordinates the divergence is
\[
\nabla \cdot \vec F =
\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} +
\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y} +
\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z} .
\tag{2.2}\]
Why do both definitions agree? Consider a small box with one corner at \((x_0, y_0, z_0)\) and edge lengths \(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z\) (Figure 2.2). On the face at \(x = x_0\) the outward normal is \(-\vec i\). If \(\vec F\) is approximately constant over this small face, the flux through it is
\[
\int_{S_1} \vec F \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec A \approx -F_1(x_0, y_0, z_0) \, \Delta y \, \Delta z .
\]
On the opposite face at \(x = x_0 + \Delta x\) the outward normal is \(+\vec i\), and the flux is \(F_1(x_0 + \Delta x, y_0, z_0) \, \Delta y \, \Delta z\). The sum of the two is
\[
\frac{F_1(x_0 + \Delta x, y_0, z_0) - F_1(x_0, y_0, z_0)}{\Delta x}
\, \Delta x \, \Delta y \, \Delta z
\approx \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} \, \Delta x \, \Delta y \, \Delta z .
\]
The other two pairs of faces contribute in the same way. Dividing the total flux by the volume \(\Delta x \, \Delta y \, \Delta z\) gives Equation 2.2.








Figure 2.2: Fluxes in the \(x\) direction through a control volume. The divergence is the net outflow per unit volume.





This derivation is more than a proof. Summing fluxes over the faces of a small box is exactly what the finite volume method does (Chapter 9).
Two results that we use constantly:
Product rule. For a scalar field \(g\) and a vector field \(\vec F\),
\[
\nabla \cdot (g \vec F) = g \, \nabla \cdot \vec F + \vec F \cdot \nabla g .
\tag{2.3}\]
Divergence theorem (Gauss). For a volume \(V\) with closed surface \(S\),
\[
\int_V \nabla \cdot \vec F \, \mathrm{d}V = \oint_S \vec F \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec A .
\tag{2.4}\]
What flows out through the surface equals the sum of all sources inside.


2.1.5 Curl and Laplacian
The curl \(\nabla \times \vec F\) measures the local rotation of a vector field. For a horizontal wind field \(\vec v = u \vec i + v \vec j\) its vertical component is the relative vorticity
\[
\zeta = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y},
\]
a central quantity of dynamic meteorology. A small paddle wheel placed in the flow and carried along with it spins with the angular velocity \(\zeta/2\): anticlockwise for \(\zeta > 0\), clockwise for \(\zeta < 0\). Figure 2.3 shows two examples. In solid-body rotation, \(u = -y\), \(v = x\), we get \(\zeta = 1 - (-1) = 2\). In the shear flow \(u = y\), \(v = 0\), we get \(\zeta = 0 - 1 = -1\). The streamlines of the shear flow are straight lines, yet the flow has vorticity: the faster flow on the upper side of the wheel pushes it clockwise. Curl measures local rotation, not curved streamlines.








Figure 2.3: Two velocity fields with vorticity, each with a paddle wheel (red) and its sense of rotation. Top: solid-body rotation, \(\zeta = 2\), anticlockwise. Bottom: shear flow with straight streamlines, \(\zeta = -1\), clockwise.





The Laplacian is the divergence of the gradient:
\[
\nabla^2 f = \nabla \cdot (\nabla f) =
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} +
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} +
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} .
\]
It compares the value of \(f\) at a point with the average over its neighbourhood. To see this, start in one dimension and take the two neighbours of \(x\) at distance \(h\). Their Taylor expansions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x + h) &= f(x) + h f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2} f''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6} f'''(x) + O(h^4), \\
f(x - h) &= f(x) - h f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2} f''(x) - \frac{h^3}{6} f'''(x) + O(h^4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding the two lines, the odd-order terms cancel:
\[
f(x + h) + f(x - h) = 2 f(x) + h^2 f''(x) + O(h^4).
\]
Dividing by 2 and subtracting \(f(x)\) gives the difference between the average of the neighbours and the value at the point:
\[
\underbrace{\frac{f(x + h) + f(x - h)}{2}}_{\text{neighbour average}} - f(x)
= \frac{h^2}{2} \, f''(x) + O(h^4).
\]
In two dimensions we do the same in the \(x\) and the \(y\) direction, with the four neighbours \((x \pm h, y)\) and \((x, y \pm h)\). Each pair gives its own second derivative, exactly as in one dimension:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x + h, y) + f(x - h, y) &= 2 f(x, y) + h^2 f_{xx} + O(h^4), \\
f(x, y + h) + f(x, y - h) &= 2 f(x, y) + h^2 f_{yy} + O(h^4).
\end{aligned}
\]
We call the average over the four neighbours \(\bar f\). Adding the two lines and dividing by 4 gives
\[
\bar f = f(x, y) + \frac{h^2}{4} \left( f_{xx} + f_{yy} \right) + O(h^4),
\]
and hence
\[
\bar f - f(x, y) = \frac{h^2}{4} \, \nabla^2 f + O(h^4).
\]
In three dimensions, with six neighbours, the factor is \(h^2/6\). So, up to a positive factor, the Laplacian is the amount by which the neighbourhood average exceeds the value at the point:

\(\nabla^2 f < 0\): \(f\) is larger than its surroundings, as at a local maximum (a peak);
\(\nabla^2 f > 0\): \(f\) is smaller than its surroundings, as at a local minimum (a trough);
\(\nabla^2 f = 0\): \(f\) equals the average of its surroundings. Such functions are called harmonic; they have no interior maxima or minima.

This is why the Laplacian appears in every equation that describes smoothing. In the diffusion equation \(\partial u/\partial t = D \nabla^2 u\) with \(D > 0\), \(u\) decreases where it lies above the average of its neighbourhood and increases where it lies below. Peaks are eroded, troughs are filled, and the field approaches its local average. Rearranged, the formula above is also the finite difference approximation
\[
\nabla^2 f \approx \frac{f(x + h, y) + f(x - h, y) + f(x, y + h) + f(x, y - h) - 4 f(x, y)}{h^2}
\]
that we will use for elliptic and parabolic problems.

title: 2  Governing equations and their classification
text:
2.2 Conservation laws
Nearly all equations of this lecture state that a quantity is conserved: mass, momentum or energy. They are all derived with the same argument.
Let \(u\) be the density of the conserved quantity (amount per volume) and \(\vec F\) its flux (amount per area and time). The amount inside a fixed volume \(V\) changes only by flux through the surface and by sources \(s\) (amount per volume and time) inside:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \int_V u \, \mathrm{d}V =
- \oint_S \vec F \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec A + \int_V s \, \mathrm{d}V .
\tag{2.5}\]
The minus sign appears because \(\mathrm{d}\vec A\) points outward. We turn this balance into a differential equation in three steps.

The volume is fixed in space, so the time derivative can be taken inside the integral: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \int_V u \, \mathrm{d}V = \int_V \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \, \mathrm{d}V\).
The divergence theorem Equation 2.4 converts the surface integral into a volume integral: \(\oint_S \vec F \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec A = \int_V \nabla \cdot \vec F \, \mathrm{d}V\).
All terms are now integrals over the same volume and can be collected:

\[
\int_V \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \vec F - s \right) \mathrm{d}V = 0 .
\]
This holds for every volume \(V\), however small and wherever it is placed. That is only possible if the integrand itself vanishes everywhere, which gives the differential form
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \vec F = s .
\tag{2.6}\]
Equation 2.6 is a prognostic equation for \(u\), but it is not yet closed, because it contains the unknown flux. A flux law (constitutive relation) expresses \(\vec F\) in terms of \(u\). Two flux laws cover most of this lecture.
Advective flux. The quantity is carried along by a velocity field \(\vec v\):
\[
\vec F = \vec v \, u .
\]
Diffusive flux. The quantity flows down its own gradient:
\[
\vec F = -D \, \nabla u .
\]
The second law has many names, depending on the quantity.

We insert the total flux \(\vec F = \vec v \, u - D \, \nabla u\) into Equation 2.6 and keep track of every sign. The divergence is linear, so it acts on the two parts separately:
\[
\nabla \cdot \vec F = \nabla \cdot (\vec v \, u) + \nabla \cdot (-D \, \nabla u)
= \nabla \cdot (\vec v \, u) - \nabla \cdot (D \, \nabla u) .
\]
Inserted into Equation 2.6:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\vec v \, u) - \nabla \cdot (D \, \nabla u) = s .
\]
Moving the diffusion term to the right-hand side changes its sign once more, which gives the advection–diffusion equation
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\vec v \, u) =
\nabla \cdot (D \, \nabla u) + s .
\tag{2.7}\]
The diffusion term now carries a plus sign. Two minus signs have cancelled: the one from the outward normal in Equation 2.5 (flux out of the volume reduces \(u\)) and the one from the flux law (the flux points down the gradient).






WarningKeep track of the signs



Lost or doubled minus signs are among the most frequent and most time-consuming errors in numerical modelling, in course projects as well as in research codes. A code with a sign error usually runs; it just gives wrong results, and the error is often found only after days of debugging. The signs depend on conventions that differ between textbooks, disciplines and codes:

Direction of the normal: outward (as here) or inward.
Flux law: \(\vec F = -D \nabla u\), or a flux defined positive in the direction of decreasing \(u\).
Vertical coordinate: \(z\) pointing up (height) or down (depth, common in hydrology and seismology). Gravity terms change sign with it.
Operator: many solvers are written for \(-\nabla^2 u = f\), because the matrix of \(-\nabla^2\) is positive definite (Chapter 4); others for \(\nabla^2 u = f\).
Source term: \(s > 0\) as a source or as a sink (e.g. extraction from a well, or evaporation).

Three habits prevent most of these errors:

Write the convention down at the top of the derivation and in the code (which direction is positive, what the flux means).
Check the physics of the result. In \(\partial u/\partial t = D \nabla^2 u\), at a maximum \(\nabla^2 u < 0\) (see the Laplacian above), so \(u\) must decrease there. With the wrong sign the maximum grows; this is anti-diffusion, and it is unstable.
Test the code on a case with a known answer: a Gaussian must spread and flatten, the total amount \(\int u \, \mathrm{d}V\) must stay constant without sources, and water must flow from high to low hydraulic head.









ImportantFlux form and advective form



With the product rule Equation 2.3 the advection term becomes \(\nabla \cdot (\vec v u) = \vec v \cdot \nabla u + u \, \nabla \cdot \vec v\). For a divergence-free (incompressible) flow the last term vanishes and the equation can be written in advective form, \(\partial u/\partial t + \vec v \cdot \nabla u = \dots\)
The two forms are mathematically equivalent. Their discretizations are not. A discretization of the flux form conserves the total amount of \(u\) exactly, because what leaves one grid cell enters its neighbour. A discretization of the advective form in general does not (Chapter 14).

2.3 Classification of differential equations

2.3.1 Ordinary and partial differential equations
If the unknown depends on one independent variable, the equation contains only ordinary derivatives and is an ordinary differential equation (ODE). An example is the equation for the charge \(Q(t)\) on a capacitor in a circuit with inductance \(L\), resistance \(R\) and capacitance \(C\):
\[
L \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 Q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + R \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \frac{1}{C} Q = E(t) .
\]
If the unknown depends on several independent variables, the equation contains partial derivatives and is a partial differential equation (PDE). The advection–diffusion equation Equation 2.7 is a PDE.


2.3.2 Systems
Several unknowns coupled by several equations form a system. The predator–prey equations
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = a x - \alpha x y, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = -c y + \gamma x y
\]
for the number of prey \(x\) and predators \(y\) are a system of two ODEs. The models of the atmosphere and the ocean are systems of PDEs, one for each prognostic variable.


2.3.3 Order
The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative in it. It determines how many initial and boundary conditions are needed.
Every ODE of order \(n\) can be rewritten as a system of \(n\) first-order ODEs. For Newton’s law Equation 1.1 we introduce the velocity \(v = \mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}t\) as a second unknown:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}t} = v, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{F}{m} .
\]
This is important in practice: numerical methods and software for ODEs are written for first-order systems. PDEs of second order in time can be treated in the same way; for seismic waves we will see that the wave equation is equivalent to a system of two first-order equations.


2.3.4 Linear and nonlinear
An equation is linear if the unknown and its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied with each other. The coefficients may depend on the independent variables. The general linear ODE of order \(n\) is
\[
a_0(t) \, y^{(n)} + a_1(t) \, y^{(n-1)} + \dots + a_n(t) \, y = g(t) .
\]
It is homogeneous if \(g(t) = 0\).

The last two rows deserve attention. Advection by a given velocity field \(c(x)\) is linear, even though the coefficient varies. Advection of the velocity by itself, as in the momentum equations of atmosphere and ocean, is nonlinear.
The pendulum equation
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + \frac{g}{L} \sin \theta = 0
\]
is nonlinear. For small angles \(\sin \theta \approx \theta\), and it becomes the linear equation of the harmonic oscillator. This linearization is a standard tool: the stability of numerical methods is analysed for linear equations, and the results are then applied to the nonlinear problem with care.
Linearity has a great practical advantage. Solutions of a linear homogeneous equation can be added (superposition), so that the solution can be analysed wave by wave (Chapter 4). Discretizing a linear PDE gives a linear system of algebraic equations; discretizing a nonlinear PDE gives a nonlinear system that has to be solved iteratively (Chapter 17).


2.3.5 Elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic
The most important classification of PDEs concerns their type. Linear second-order PDEs in two independent variables have the general form
\[
a \, u_{xx} + 2 b \, u_{xy} + c \, u_{yy} + \text{lower-order terms} = f ,
\tag{2.8}\]
where the second variable \(y\) may be a space coordinate or time. The type is determined by the coefficients of the second derivatives alone:









Type
Condition
Prototype

Laplace, Poisson: \(u_{xx} + u_{yy} = f\)

Diffusion: \(u_t = D u_{xx}\)

Wave: \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\)

The names come from the quadratic form \(q(x, y) = a x^2 + 2 b x y + c y^2\), whose contour \(q = 1\) is an ellipse or a hyperbola under the first and third condition. In matrix notation,
\[
q(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} x & y \end{pmatrix} A \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix},
\]
and the condition can be read off the signs of the eigenvalues of \(A\). To see why, we compute the eigenvalues. They are the roots of the characteristic polynomial
\[
\det(A - \lambda I) =
\begin{vmatrix} a - \lambda & b \\ b & c - \lambda \end{vmatrix}
= (a - \lambda)(c - \lambda) - b^2
= \lambda^2 - (a + c) \, \lambda + (ac - b^2) .
\]
A quadratic polynomial with roots \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) can be written as \((\lambda - \lambda_1)(\lambda - \lambda_2) = \lambda^2 - (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) \lambda + \lambda_1 \lambda_2\). Comparing the coefficients gives
\[
\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = a + c , \qquad
\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = ac - b^2 = \det A .
\]
The eigenvalues are real, because \(A\) is symmetric. The discriminant of the characteristic polynomial confirms this: \((a + c)^2 - 4(ac - b^2) = (a - c)^2 + 4 b^2 \ge 0\). The sign of the product \(\lambda_1 \lambda_2\) therefore decides the type, and it is the opposite of the sign of \(b^2 - ac\):

\(b^2 - ac < 0\): \(\lambda_1 \lambda_2 > 0\), both eigenvalues have the same sign (elliptic);
\(b^2 - ac = 0\): \(\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = 0\), one eigenvalue is zero (parabolic);
\(b^2 - ac > 0\): \(\lambda_1 \lambda_2 < 0\), the eigenvalues have opposite signs (hyperbolic).

The geometric meaning follows from the eigenvectors. Because \(A\) is symmetric, its eigenvectors are orthogonal, and in coordinates \((\xi, \eta)\) along the eigenvectors the mixed term disappears:
\[
q = \lambda_1 \xi^2 + \lambda_2 \eta^2 .
\]
For \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0\) the contour \(q = 1\) is an ellipse with semi-axes \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}\) and \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}\). For eigenvalues of opposite sign it is a hyperbola. If \(\lambda_2 = 0\), \(q = \lambda_1 \xi^2\) does not depend on \(\eta\) at all, and \(q = 1\) degenerates into two parallel lines, the limiting case between ellipse and hyperbola. The same rotation of coordinates applied to the PDE removes the mixed derivative and gives its canonical form \(\lambda_1 u_{\xi\xi} + \lambda_2 u_{\eta\eta} + \text{lower-order terms} = f\). Elliptic equations then look like the Poisson equation, hyperbolic ones like the wave equation, and parabolic ones contain only one second derivative, like the diffusion equation.
As an example, take \(u_{xx} + 4 u_{xy} + u_{yy} = 0\), that is \(a = c = 1\) and \(b = 2\). The condition gives \(b^2 - ac = 4 - 1 = 3 > 0\): hyperbolic. The eigenvalues confirm this: \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 2\) and \(\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = 1 - 4 = -3\), so \(\lambda_1 = 3\) and \(\lambda_2 = -1\), of opposite sign. The mixed derivative hides the type: both pure second derivatives have the same sign, yet the equation is a wave equation in rotated coordinates.
The eigenvalue formulation carries over to more than two variables, where the condition \(b^2 - ac\) no longer exists (Wick 2020). With \(n\) independent variables, \(A\) is a symmetric \(n \times n\) matrix. The equation is elliptic if all eigenvalues have the same sign, parabolic if one eigenvalue is zero and the others have the same sign, and hyperbolic if one eigenvalue has the opposite sign of the others. The heat equation \(u_t = D (u_{xx} + u_{yy})\) in the variables \((x, y, t)\), for example, has the eigenvalues \(D\), \(D\) and \(0\) (up to an overall sign): parabolic. We meet quadratic forms again when we solve linear systems by minimisation (Chapter 11).






TipCheck: classify the diffusion equation with this rule





Write \(u_t - D u_{xx} = 0\) with the variables \((x, t)\) in the form Equation 2.8. The only second derivative is \(u_{xx}\) with \(a = -D\), and \(b = c = 0\). Hence \(b^2 - ac = 0\): parabolic. For the wave equation \(u_{tt} - c_0^2 u_{xx} = 0\) we have \(a = -c_0^2\), \(b = 0\), \(c = 1\) and \(b^2 - ac = c_0^2 > 0\): hyperbolic.



What the three types mean physically is shown by their prototypes in the next section.

title: 2  Governing equations and their classification
text:
2.4 Prototype equations
Three special cases of conservation laws in one space dimension serve as prototypes, one for each type of the classification. Each has its own physical behaviour, and each requires its own numerical treatment.
Diffusion equation (heat equation), from Equation 2.7 with \(\vec v = 0\) and constant \(D\); parabolic:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{2.9}\]
Advection equation, with constant velocity \(c\) and \(D = 0\); of first order and hyperbolic:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0 .
\tag{2.10}\]
Wave equation, with wave speed \(c\); hyperbolic:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{2.11}\]
On an unbounded domain all three have exact solutions for the initial condition \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\).
Advection. The solution is \(u(x, t) = f(x - ct)\): the initial shape moves with velocity \(c\) and does not change. Information travels along the lines \(x - ct = \text{const}\), the characteristics of the equation, with the finite speed \(c\); first-order equations with this property are called hyperbolic, like the wave equation. To verify the solution, set \(\xi = x - ct\) and apply the chain rule:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = f'(\xi) \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial t} = -c \, f'(\xi), \qquad
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = f'(\xi) \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial x} = f'(\xi)
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0 .
\]
This verifies the solution but does not tell us where it comes from. The box derives it.






NoteDerivation: the method of characteristics



We look at \(u\) along a curve \(x(t)\) in the \((x, t)\) plane, that is at the function \(U(t) = u(x(t), t)\). Its rate of change follows from the chain rule for a function of two variables, both of which depend on \(t\):
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t}
= \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}t}
= \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \, \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} .
\]
The right-hand side looks like the left-hand side of Equation 2.10. We choose the curve such that the two agree, that is with
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = c .
\]
Integrating from \(t = 0\), where the curve starts at the point \(x_0\), gives the straight line \(x(t) = x_0 + c t\). Along this line the PDE becomes an ODE:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t}
= \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c \, \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0 .
\]
So \(U\) does not change, and \(u\) keeps the value it had at the starting point:
\[
u(x_0 + c t, t) = U(t) = U(0) = u(x_0, 0) = f(x_0) .
\]
Finally we express \(x_0\) by the point \((x, t)\) we are interested in. The characteristic through \((x, t)\) started at \(x_0 = x - c t\), hence
\[
u(x, t) = f(x - c t) .
\]
The derivation shows more than the verification:

Uniqueness. Every point \((x, t)\) lies on exactly one characteristic, and the value there is fixed by the initial condition. There is no other solution.
Domain of dependence. \(u(x, t)\) depends only on the initial value at the single point \(x - ct\), not on \(f\) anywhere else. Information travels along the characteristics with speed \(c\).
Generalisation. The same steps work for a variable velocity \(c(x, t)\): the characteristics are the solutions of the ODE \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t = c(x, t)\), are no longer straight, and \(u\) is still constant along them. We return to this view of advection in the semi-Lagrangian methods (Chapter 14).



Wave equation. Differentiating once more gives \(\partial^2 u / \partial t^2 = c^2 f''(\xi)\) and \(\partial^2 u / \partial x^2 = f''(\xi)\), so \(f(x - ct)\) also solves the wave equation. The sign of \(c\) drops out in the second derivative, so \(f(x + ct)\) is a solution as well. For zero initial velocity the solution is \(u(x, t) = \tfrac12 [f(x - ct) + f(x + ct)]\): the initial shape splits into two halves that travel in opposite directions. At \(t = 0\) the two halves add up to \(f(x)\), and their time derivatives, \(\mp \tfrac12 c f'(x)\), cancel.
Diffusion. For the Gaussian initial condition \(f(x) = e^{-x^2 / w^2}\) the solution remains a Gaussian that widens and flattens,
\[
u(x, t) = \frac{w}{\sqrt{w^2 + 4 D t}} \exp \left( - \frac{x^2}{w^2 + 4 D t} \right) .
\]
The squared width grows linearly in time, \(w^2 + 4Dt\), and the amplitude decreases such that the integral of \(u\), the total amount, stays constant.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(-10, 10, 801)
w = 1.0                       # width of the initial Gaussian
f = lambda x: np.exp(-(x / w) ** 2)
D, c = 1.0, 1.0

def diffusion(x, t):
    return w / np.sqrt(w**2 + 4 * D * t) * np.exp(-x**2 / (w**2 + 4 * D * t))

solutions = {
    "Diffusion": diffusion,
    "Advection": lambda x, t: f(x - c * t),
    "Wave": lambda x, t: 0.5 * (f(x - c * t) + f(x + c * t)),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 2.8), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, u) in zip(axes, solutions.items()):
    ax.plot(x, f(x), "k", label="$t = 0$")
    for t in [2, 4, 6]:
        ax.plot(x, u(x, t), label=f"$t = {t}$")
    ax.set_title(name)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("$u$")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2.4: Exact solutions of the three prototype equations for the same Gaussian initial condition (black) at three later times.





Figure 2.4 contains the most important physical distinction of this lecture. Diffusion smooths and has no direction. Advection and waves transport information with a finite speed and preserve the shape. A good numerical method must reproduce this behaviour: it must not move a diffusing profile, and it must not smear or distort a travelling one. The second requirement turns out to be the harder one (Chapter 13).
A fourth prototype, the elliptic one, has no time derivative. In steady state, \(\partial u / \partial t = 0\), the diffusion equation with a source becomes the Poisson equation
\[
- \nabla^2 u = f ,
\tag{2.12}\]
and for \(f = 0\) the Laplace equation. It describes equilibria: steady temperature and groundwater fields, the gravitational potential, the pressure in an incompressible fluid.

text:
2.5 The equations of this lecture
The equations of real models are combinations of the prototypes. We list the ones that appear in later units, so that you recognise the building blocks.
Shallow water equations. A layer of fluid of depth \(h\) and velocity \(u\) over a flat bottom, in one dimension and without rotation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (h u)}{\partial x} &= 0, \\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + g \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} &= 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.13}\]
The first equation is conservation of mass in flux form, the second is conservation of momentum in advective form. The system is nonlinear.
To see what it describes we linearize it about a state of rest with depth \(H\). We write \(h = H + \eta\) and assume that the surface elevation \(\eta\) and the velocity \(u\) are small, so that products of small quantities can be neglected: \(h u \approx H u\) and \(u \, \partial u / \partial x \approx 0\). What remains is
\[
\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} + H \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0, \qquad
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + g \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x} = 0 .
\tag{2.14}\]
These are two first-order equations for two unknowns. We combine them into one second-order equation for \(\eta\) alone by eliminating \(u\). The two equations are coupled through derivatives of \(u\): the first contains \(\partial u / \partial x\), the second \(\partial u / \partial t\). Differentiating the first equation with respect to \(t\) and the second with respect to \(x\) produces the same mixed derivative of \(u\) in both. Since \(H\) and \(g\) are constants, they stay in front of the derivatives:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial t^2} + H \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t \, \partial x} = 0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \, \partial t} + g \frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial x^2} = 0 .
\]
For smooth functions the order of differentiation does not matter (Schwarz’s theorem), so \(\partial^2 u / \partial t \, \partial x = \partial^2 u / \partial x \, \partial t\). The second equation gives this mixed derivative in terms of \(\eta\):
\[
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \, \partial t} = - g \frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial x^2} .
\]
Inserting it into the first equation,
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial t^2} + H \left( - g \frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial x^2} \right) = 0 ,
\]
and moving the second term to the right-hand side gives
\[
\frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial t^2} = g H \frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial x^2} ,
\]
the wave equation Equation 2.11 with \(c = \sqrt{g H}\). The shallow water equations describe gravity waves; they are a hyperbolic system. Note how the signs work out: the minus sign from solving the second equation for the mixed derivative and the one from moving the term to the right-hand side combine to \(+gH\). Since \(g H > 0\) the result is a wave equation; with \(-gH\) it would be elliptic, and there would be no waves. Eliminating \(\eta\) instead, by differentiating the first equation with respect to \(x\) and the second with respect to \(t\), gives the same wave equation for \(u\). For an ocean of depth 4 km, \(c = \sqrt{9.81 \cdot 4000}\) m/s \(\approx 200\) m/s, the speed of a tsunami. With rotation added the system contains much of the dynamics of the atmosphere and the ocean, which makes it the standard test bed for the numerical methods of weather and climate models (Chapter 15).
What makes a system of first-order equations hyperbolic? A first-order system
\[
\frac{\partial \vec q}{\partial t} + B \frac{\partial \vec q}{\partial x} = 0
\]
is hyperbolic if the matrix \(B\) has real eigenvalues and a full set of eigenvectors. It can then be decomposed into advection equations, one for each eigenvalue, and the eigenvalues are the speeds.
For the linearized shallow water equations Equation 2.14, \(\vec q = (\eta, u)^T\) and
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & H \\ g & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\det (B - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - g H = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda = \pm \sqrt{g H} .
\]
The two eigenvalues are the speeds of the gravity waves travelling to the right and to the left. For the full equations Equation 2.13 the same calculation gives \(u \pm \sqrt{g h}\): the waves are in addition carried by the flow.
Primitive equations. The equations of atmospheric and ocean models are the conservation laws for momentum, mass and energy of a stratified fluid on the rotating sphere, with the hydrostatic approximation in the vertical. Each is an advection equation for one prognostic variable with source terms: pressure gradient and Coriolis force for momentum, heating for temperature, phase changes for humidity. Their dynamics are dominated by advection and waves, that is, by hyperbolic behaviour; diffusion terms represent the mixing by turbulence.
Groundwater flow. Conservation of mass with Darcy’s law gives a diffusion equation for the hydraulic head \(h\),
\[
S_s \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (K \, \nabla h) + q ,
\tag{2.15}\]
with specific storage \(S_s\), hydraulic conductivity \(K\) and sources \(q\). It is parabolic, and in steady state elliptic. \(K\) varies in space over many orders of magnitude, which is the main numerical difficulty (Chapter 9).
Richards equation. In the unsaturated soil, water content \(\theta\) and hydraulic conductivity \(K\) depend on the pressure head \(\psi\):
\[
\frac{\partial \theta(\psi)}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot \left[ K(\psi) \, \nabla (\psi + z) \right] .
\tag{2.16}\]
The equation is a parabolic diffusion equation whose coefficients depend strongly on the solution. It is the prototype of a nonlinear problem in this lecture (Chapter 17).
Seismic waves. Conservation of momentum with Hooke’s law gives, for a shear wave propagating in the \(x\) direction with particle velocity \(v\) and shear stress \(\sigma\),
\[
\rho \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial x}, \qquad
\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial t} = \mu \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} ,
\tag{2.17}\]
with density \(\rho\) and shear modulus \(\mu\). For constant \(\rho\) and \(\mu\) we differentiate the first equation with respect to \(t\) and insert the second:
\[
\rho \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial t^2}
= \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial t}
= \mu \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2}
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\mu}{\rho} \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} .
\]
This is the wave equation Equation 2.11 with the shear wave speed \(c = \sqrt{\mu / \rho}\), and Equation 2.17 is a hyperbolic system. The structure is the same as in Equation 2.14: two first-order equations for two variables that drive each other.
Real models mix the types. The advection–diffusion equation Equation 2.7 is formally parabolic, but behaves like a hyperbolic equation when advection dominates. The same holds for the Navier–Stokes equations at high Reynolds number. Numerical models therefore often treat the terms of one equation with different methods (Chapter 18).

2.6 Initial and boundary conditions
A differential equation has many solutions. Initial and boundary conditions select one.
Initial conditions prescribe the state at \(t = 0\). Their number equals the order of the time derivative: one for the diffusion equation, \(u(x, 0) = u_0(x)\), and two for the wave equation, \(u(x, 0)\) and \(u_t(x, 0)\).
Boundary conditions prescribe the behaviour on the boundary \(\partial\Omega\) of the domain \(\Omega\). For second-order equations three types are used, where \(\partial u / \partial n\) is the derivative in the direction of the outward normal.

A condition with \(g = 0\) is called homogeneous. On each part of the boundary exactly one condition is prescribed.
A fourth kind is common in atmospheric modelling: periodic boundary conditions, \(u(0, t) = u(L, t)\). On a latitude circle they are exact. Limited-area models face the opposite situation: their lateral boundaries are artificial, and waves must be able to leave the domain without reflection. Such open boundaries are a subject of their own (Chapter 16).

text:
2.7 Well-posed problems
A problem is well-posed in the sense of Hadamard1 if

a solution exists,
the solution is unique,
the solution depends continuously on the data, that is on initial conditions, boundary conditions and parameters.

If one of the conditions is violated, a numerical solution is meaningless or impossible. Three examples show that this is of practical relevance.
Too few conditions. The Poisson equation with Neumann conditions on the whole boundary prescribes only fluxes. If \(u\) is a solution, so is \(u\) plus any constant, which violates condition 2. Moreover a solution exists only if the prescribed boundary fluxes balance the sources, which concerns condition 1. In the discrete problem this shows up as a singular matrix.
The wrong direction of time. The diffusion equation smooths. Solving it backward in time, in order to find the initial state that led to an observed state, must therefore roughen: small-scale errors in the observed state are amplified without bound, which violates condition 3. Problems of this kind, where causes are inferred from effects, are the inverse problems of geophysics and the data assimilation problem of meteorology. They need additional information to become well-posed (Chapter 21).
The wrong kind of conditions. Hadamard’s own example shows that the conditions must match the type of the equation. Take the Laplace equation in the upper half plane \(y > 0\) and prescribe, as for the wave equation, the value and the normal derivative on the line \(y = 0\):
\[
u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0, \qquad
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad
u_y(x, 0) = \frac{1}{n} \sin(n x) .
\]
We look for a solution of the form \(u = \sin(n x) \, Y(y)\). Inserting it, \(u_{xx} = -n^2 \sin(n x) \, Y\) and \(u_{yy} = \sin(n x) \, Y''\), so the PDE becomes the ODE \(Y'' = n^2 Y\) with the general solution \(Y = A \cosh(n y) + B \sinh(n y)\). The first condition gives \(Y(0) = A = 0\). The second gives \(Y'(0) = n B = 1/n\), so \(B = 1/n^2\) and
\[
u(x, y) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sin(n x) \sinh(n y) .
\]
Now let \(n \to \infty\). The data tend to zero, \(|u_y(x, 0)| \le 1/n\), and for zero data the solution is \(u = 0\). But at any fixed height \(y > 0\) the solution grows without bound, since \(\sinh(n y) \approx \tfrac12 e^{n y}\): at \(y = 1\) and \(n = 20\), data of size \(0.05\) produce a solution of size \(\tfrac{1}{400} \sinh(20) \approx 6 \cdot 10^5\). Condition 3 is violated.
The same data are harmless for the wave equation \(u_{tt} = u_{xx}\) with \(t\) in place of \(y\). There the ODE is \(Y'' = -n^2 Y\), the hyperbolic functions become trigonometric ones, and the solution \(u = \frac{1}{n^2} \sin(n x) \sin(n t)\) stays below \(1/n^2\). The only difference is the sign in front of \(n^2\), and that sign is the type of the equation. An elliptic equation needs one condition on the whole boundary, not two conditions on part of it (see the table in Section 2.4). In geophysics this example appears as the downward continuation of gravity and magnetic fields: computing the field at depth from measurements at the surface amplifies the short wavelengths exponentially.
Condition 3 for the mathematical problem has a counterpart for the numerical method: stability (Chapter 6). And well-posed does not mean predictable for all times. The equations of the atmosphere are well-posed, yet small errors in the initial state grow so fast that the forecast loses its value after about two weeks (Chapter 8).

2.8 Summary

Gradient, divergence, curl and Laplacian are the building blocks of all equations in this lecture. The divergence is the net outflow per volume.
A conservation law states that the amount in a volume changes only by the flux through its surface and by sources: \(\partial u / \partial t + \nabla \cdot \vec F = s\). Advective and diffusive fluxes close the equation.
Classify before you compute: ODE or PDE, order, linear or nonlinear, elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic. The type decides the numerical method.
The prototypes show what the types mean: diffusion smooths; advection and waves propagate with finite speed; the Poisson equation describes equilibria.
The equations of atmospheric, hydrological and seismic models are combinations of the prototypes, and each can be classified the same way.
A well-posed problem has the right number of initial and boundary conditions, and its solution depends continuously on the data.

3.1 Taylor series and finite differences
Numerical models are built from a small number of tools. This unit introduces the tools that come from calculus: approximating derivatives, interpolating, integrating and finding roots. All of them rest on the Taylor series. The next unit adds the tools from linear algebra and Fourier analysis.

title: 3  The numerical toolbox I: derivatives, integrals, roots
text:
3.1.1 The Taylor series
The Taylor series expresses the value of a smooth function at a neighbouring point by its value and its derivatives at \(x\):
\[
u(x + h) = u(x) + h \, u'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2} u''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6} u'''(x) + \frac{h^4}{24} u''''(x) + \dots
\tag{3.1}\]
The general term is \(\frac{h^k}{k!} u^{(k)}(x)\), with \(2! = 2\), \(3! = 6\), \(4! = 24\). If the series is stopped after the term with \(h^n\), the rest can be written as a single term,
\[
u(x + h) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{h^k}{k!} u^{(k)}(x) + \frac{h^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} u^{(n+1)}(\xi)
\]
with some \(\xi\) between \(x\) and \(x + h\) (Lagrange form of the remainder). This is what makes the dots precise: the neglected part behaves like the first neglected term, provided \(u^{(n+1)}\) is bounded. “Smooth” means that the derivatives that appear exist and are bounded.
Replacing \(h\) by \(-h\) changes the sign of the odd terms, because \((-h)^k = -h^k\) for odd \(k\):
\[
u(x - h) = u(x) - h \, u'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2} u''(x) - \frac{h^3}{6} u'''(x) + \frac{h^4}{24} u''''(x) - \dots
\tag{3.2}\]
Every finite difference formula is a combination of such series, chosen so that unwanted terms cancel.
Notation. We write \(e = O(h^p)\), “\(e\) is of order \(h^p\)”, if \(|e| \le C h^p\) for all sufficiently small \(h\), with a constant \(C\) that does not depend on \(h\). A method whose error is \(O(h^p)\) is of order \(p\). Halving \(h\) then divides the error by about \(2^p\).


3.1.2 Forward and backward difference
We solve Equation 3.1 for \(u'(x)\). Subtracting \(u(x)\) on both sides gives
\[
u(x + h) - u(x) = h \, u'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2} u''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6} u'''(x) + \dots ,
\]
and dividing by \(h\)
\[
\frac{u(x + h) - u(x)}{h} = u'(x) + \frac{h}{2} u''(x) + \frac{h^2}{6} u'''(x) + \dots .
\]
Bringing everything except \(u'(x)\) to the other side,
\[
u'(x) = \underbrace{\frac{u(x + h) - u(x)}{h}}_{\text{forward difference}}
\; \underbrace{- \, \frac{h}{2} u''(x) - \frac{h^2}{6} u'''(x) - \dots}_{\text{truncation error}}
\tag{3.3}\]
The terms that are dropped when only the difference quotient is kept form the truncation error. Its leading term is \(-\frac{h}{2} u''(x)\), proportional to \(h\). The forward difference is of first order: its error is \(O(h)\).
The same steps applied to Equation 3.2 give
\[
u(x) - u(x - h) = h \, u'(x) - \frac{h^2}{2} u''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6} u'''(x) - \dots ,
\]
and after division by \(h\) the backward difference
\[
u'(x) = \frac{u(x) - u(x - h)}{h} + \frac{h}{2} u''(x) - \frac{h^2}{6} u'''(x) + \dots ,
\tag{3.4}\]
which is also of first order, with the opposite sign of the leading error.


3.1.3 Central difference
The errors of the two one-sided formulas have opposite signs, which suggests combining them. We subtract Equation 3.2 from Equation 3.1 term by term:

All even terms cancel:
\[
u(x + h) - u(x - h) = 2 h \, u'(x) + \frac{h^3}{3} u'''(x) + \dots
\]
Dividing by \(2h\) gives \(\frac{u(x + h) - u(x - h)}{2h} = u'(x) + \frac{h^2}{6} u'''(x) + \dots\), and solving for \(u'(x)\) the central difference
\[
u'(x) = \frac{u(x + h) - u(x - h)}{2h} - \frac{h^2}{6} u'''(x) - \dots
\tag{3.5}\]
Its error is \(O(h^2)\): second order. Halving \(h\) halves the error of the one-sided differences but quarters the error of the central difference, at the same cost of two function values.


3.1.4 Second derivative
Adding the two series instead cancels the odd terms (last column of the table, with the signs of \(u(x - h)\) reversed):
\[
u(x + h) + u(x - h) = 2 u(x) + h^2 u''(x) + \frac{h^4}{12} u''''(x) + \dots ,
\]
where \(\frac{h^4}{12} = 2 \cdot \frac{h^4}{24}\). Subtracting \(2 u(x)\) gives \(u(x + h) - 2 u(x) + u(x - h) = h^2 u''(x) + \frac{h^4}{12} u''''(x) + \dots\), and dividing by \(h^2\) and solving for \(u''(x)\) gives the standard approximation of the second derivative,
\[
u''(x) = \frac{u(x + h) - 2 u(x) + u(x - h)}{h^2} - \frac{h^2}{12} u''''(x) - \dots ,
\tag{3.6}\]
which is also of second order. This formula is the core of every finite difference model of diffusion.
There is a second way to obtain it, which becomes important when the diffusion coefficient varies in space. The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative. We approximate the first derivative half-way between the grid points,
\[
u'\!\left(x + \tfrac{h}{2}\right) \approx \frac{u(x + h) - u(x)}{h}, \qquad
u'\!\left(x - \tfrac{h}{2}\right) \approx \frac{u(x) - u(x - h)}{h} .
\]
Seen from the point \(x + \tfrac{h}{2}\), the first quotient uses the two neighbours at distance \(\tfrac{h}{2}\) on either side: it is a central difference with step \(h/2\) and therefore of second order. The same holds for the second quotient at \(x - \tfrac{h}{2}\). We then take the central difference of these two values, again with step \(h/2\):
\[
u''(x) \approx \frac{u'\!\left(x + \tfrac{h}{2}\right) - u'\!\left(x - \tfrac{h}{2}\right)}{h}
= \frac{1}{h} \left[ \frac{u(x + h) - u(x)}{h} - \frac{u(x) - u(x - h)}{h} \right]
= \frac{u(x + h) - 2 u(x) + u(x - h)}{h^2} .
\]
In this form the formula is a difference of two fluxes, as in the derivation of the divergence in Chapter 2.


3.1.5 Measuring the order of convergence
If the error behaves as \(e(h) \approx C h^p\), then taking the logarithm gives
\[
\log e = \log C + p \log h .
\]
In a plot with logarithmic axes the error is a straight line with slope \(p\). To compute \(p\) from two step sizes \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) we divide the two errors. The unknown constant \(C\) drops out,
\[
\frac{e(h_1)}{e(h_2)} = \frac{C h_1^p}{C h_2^p} = \left( \frac{h_1}{h_2} \right)^p ,
\]
and taking the logarithm of both sides, \(\log \left( e(h_1) / e(h_2) \right) = p \log (h_1 / h_2)\), gives the observed order
\[
p = \frac{\log \left( e(h_1) / e(h_2) \right)}{\log \left( h_1 / h_2 \right)} .
\tag{3.7}\]
If the step is halved, \(h_1 / h_2 = 2\) and \(p = \log_2 \left( e(h_1) / e(h_2) \right)\): an error that falls by a factor of 4 means second order.
Comparing the observed order with the theoretical one is the most important test of a numerical code. A bug almost always reduces the order. We test the forward and central difference with \(u = \sin\), whose derivative \(\cos\) is known, at \(x = 1\).

Step by stepCompact



import numpy as np                  # NumPy: np.sin, np.cos, np.log, ...

x = 1.0                             # point where we approximate u'(x)
exact = np.cos(x)                   # exact derivative of sin at x

3.1.6 Why the step cannot be made arbitrarily small
According to Equation 3.3 the error vanishes for \(h \to 0\). On a computer it does not, and we can estimate why.
The computer does not hold \(u(x)\) and \(u(x + h)\) but rounded values \(u(x)(1 + \delta_1)\) and \(u(x + h)(1 + \delta_2)\) with \(|\delta_{1,2}| \le \varepsilon\), the machine epsilon (Chapter 1). The computed numerator is
\[
u(x + h)(1 + \delta_2) - u(x)(1 + \delta_1)
= \big[ u(x + h) - u(x) \big] + u(x + h) \, \delta_2 - u(x) \, \delta_1 ,
\]
so it differs from the exact numerator by
\[
|u(x + h) \, \delta_2 - u(x) \, \delta_1| \le \varepsilon \, \big( |u(x + h)| + |u(x)| \big) \approx 2 \varepsilon |u| ,
\]
where we used \(u(x + h) \approx u(x)\) for small \(h\) and wrote \(|u|\) for \(|u(x)|\). The division by \(h\) is itself accurate to \(\varepsilon\), but it turns this absolute error of the numerator into an error of \(2 \varepsilon |u| / h\) in the difference quotient: the smaller \(h\), the larger the error. Together with the leading truncation error from Equation 3.3 the total error of the forward difference is bounded by
\[
e(h) = \underbrace{\frac{h}{2} |u''|}_{\text{truncation}} +
\underbrace{\frac{2 \varepsilon |u|}{h}}_{\text{round-off}} .
\tag{3.8}\]
The first term decreases with \(h\), the second increases. The minimum is where the derivative with respect to \(h\) vanishes:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}e}{\mathrm{d}h} = \frac{|u''|}{2} - \frac{2 \varepsilon |u|}{h^2} = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
h^2 = \frac{4 \varepsilon |u|}{|u''|}
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
h_{\text{opt}} = 2 \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon |u|}{|u''|}} .
\]
Inserting \(h_{\text{opt}}\) into Equation 3.8, both terms become equal,
\[
\frac{h_{\text{opt}}}{2} |u''| = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon |u|}{|u''|}} \, |u''| = \sqrt{\varepsilon |u| |u''|},
\qquad
\frac{2 \varepsilon |u|}{h_{\text{opt}}} = \varepsilon |u| \sqrt{\frac{|u''|}{\varepsilon |u|}} = \sqrt{\varepsilon |u| |u''|},
\]
and the smallest error is their sum,
\[
e(h_{\text{opt}}) = 2 \sqrt{\varepsilon \, |u| \, |u''|} .
\]
If \(u\) and \(u''\) are of order one, the best step is of the order \(\sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}\), and the smallest error that can be reached is also about \(10^{-8}\): half of the 16 digits are lost.
For the central difference the numerator has the same round-off error \(2 \varepsilon |u|\), but it is divided by \(2h\), which gives \(\varepsilon |u| / h\). With the truncation error \(\frac{h^2}{6} |u'''|\) from Equation 3.5,
\[
e(h) = \frac{h^2}{6} |u'''| + \frac{\varepsilon |u|}{h}, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}e}{\mathrm{d}h} = \frac{h}{3} |u'''| - \frac{\varepsilon |u|}{h^2} = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
h_{\text{opt}} = \left( \frac{3 \varepsilon |u|}{|u'''|} \right)^{1/3} .
\]
At \(h_{\text{opt}}\) we have \(\varepsilon |u| = \frac13 h_{\text{opt}}^3 |u'''|\), so the round-off term is \(\frac13 h_{\text{opt}}^2 |u'''|\), twice the truncation term, and
\[
e(h_{\text{opt}}) = \frac{h_{\text{opt}}^2}{6} |u'''| + \frac{h_{\text{opt}}^2}{3} |u'''|
= \frac{h_{\text{opt}}^2}{2} |u'''| .
\]
For \(u\) and \(u'''\) of order one, \(h_{\text{opt}} \sim \varepsilon^{1/3} \approx 10^{-5}\) and \(e(h_{\text{opt}}) \sim \varepsilon^{2/3} \approx 10^{-11}\).

Figure 3.1 confirms the estimates: the error of the forward difference stops decreasing near \(h = 10^{-8}\), at about \(10^{-8}\), that of the central difference near \(h = 10^{-5}\), at about \(10^{-11}\). Single points can lie lower, where the rounding errors happen to cancel; the estimates are bounds for the typical error. Left of the optimum the error grows like \(1/h\) and scatters, because the rounding errors \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\) vary irregularly from one \(h\) to the next. The figure has two lessons. First, a higher order gives a smaller error for the same step and is less affected by round-off. Second, in a convergence test the step must be neither so large that higher-order terms disturb the slope nor so small that round-off dominates.


3.1.7 Stencils of any order
The points used by a difference formula form its stencil. Formulas for any stencil and any derivative follow from one recipe, the method of undetermined coefficients. We look for weights \(w_j\) such that
\[
\sum_j w_j \, u(x + s_j h) \approx u^{(m)}(x),
\]
where the offsets \(s_j\) define the stencil.
Worked example. We want the first derivative at a boundary point \(x\), where only the points \(x\), \(x + h\) and \(x + 2h\) are available: offsets \(s = (0, 1, 2)\). We write the Taylor series of the three values,
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x) &= u(x), \\
u(x + h) &= u(x) + h \, u'(x) + \tfrac12 h^2 u''(x) + \tfrac16 h^3 u'''(x) + \dots, \\
u(x + 2h) &= u(x) + 2h \, u'(x) + \tfrac{(2h)^2}{2} u''(x) + \tfrac{(2h)^3}{6} u'''(x) + \dots \\
&= u(x) + 2h \, u'(x) + 2 h^2 u''(x) + \tfrac86 h^3 u'''(x) + \dots ,
\end{aligned}
\]
and collect, for each derivative of \(u\), the factor with which it appears:
